questions.qtext:
​​​​​The relation schema, Person (pid, city), describes the city of residence for every person uniquely identified by pid. The following relational algebra operators are available: selection, projection, cross product, and rename.

To find the list of cities where at least $3$ persons reside, using the above operators, the minimum number of cross product operations that must be used is
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 4)

Relational Algebra expression looks like this

Condition 1: c1: $(city1 = city2) \land (city2 = city3) \land (city3 = city1)$

Condition 2: c2: $(pid1 <> pid2) \land (pid2 <> pid3) \land (pid1 <> pid3)$

$\pi_{city1} [\sigma_{c1 \land c2} (\rho_{(pid1,city1)}(Person) \times \rho_{(pid2,city2)}(Person) \times \rho_{(pid3,city3)}(Person))]$

Here, two cross joins are used. Hence, Answer is 2.

Answer: B

Detailed Video Solution (Click Here)

Source solution 2 (score: 6)

To find the list of cities where at least $3$ persons reside, we need to do cross product of 3 tables, So, minimum only 2 cross products are required.

questions.qtext: Given two union compatible relations $R_1(A, B)$ and $R_2 (C, D)$, what is the result of the operation $R_1 \Join_{ A = C \wedge B = D} R_2$?
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 1)
Answer is option $\boxed{D}$

What the conditional join is doing is basically for each tuple in $R_1$ is compared with each tuple of $R_2$ and if corresponding attribute values are equal then the tuple would be in the final result.

This is bascailly what intersection operation does.

questions.qtext: What is the optimized version of the relation algebra expression $\pi_{A1}(\pi_{A2}(\sigma_{F1}(\sigma_{F2}(r))))$, where $A1, A2$ are sets of attributes in $r$ with $A1 \subset A2$ and $F1,F2$ are Boolean expressions based on the attributes in $r$?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 6)

σF1 (σF2 (r)) ≡ σF1∧F2 (Cascading of Selection)

so options B and D are Incorrect.

πA1 ( πA2 (r) ) ≡ πA1 when A1 ⊆ A2 (Cascading of Projection)

So From Options A and C, only A is following both the rules.

so option A is correct.

-

\]

questions.qtext:
The following relation records the age of $500$ employees of a company, where $empNo$ (indicating the employee number) is the key:

$$empAge(\underline{empNo},age)$$

Consider the following relational algebra expression:

$$\Pi_{empNo}(empAge \Join_{(age>age1)} \rho_{empNo1,age1}(empAge))$$

What does the above expression generate?

options.text: Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is the maximum
Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is more than the age of exactly one other employee
Employee numbers of all employees whose age is not the minimum
Employee numbers of all employees whose age is the minimum

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 1)

The expression provided is:

$$\Pi_{empNo}(empAge \bowtie_{(age > age1)} \rho_{empNo1, age1}(empAge))$$

To understand what this generates, let's break down the operations:

  1. Renaming ($\rho$): The expression $\rho_{empNo1, age1}(empAge)$ creates a copy of the empAge table with renamed columns ($empNo1, age1$).

  2. Theta Join ($\bowtie_{(age > age1)}$): This joins the original table with its copy where the original employee's age is strictly greater than some other employee's age ($age1$).

    • If an employee has the absolute minimum age in the company, their age will never be greater than any age1 from the second table.

    • Therefore, an employee with the minimum age will never satisfy the join condition and will be excluded from the result.

  3. Projection ($\Pi$): This returns the employee numbers ($empNo$) of everyone who successfully satisfied the join condition.

Conclusion

Since the join condition ($age > age1$) only keeps employees who are older than at least one other person, it effectively filters out anyone who holds the minimum age.

The correct answer is C: Employee numbers of all employees whose age is not the minimum.

questions.qtext:
​​​​​Consider a database that includes the following relations:

Defender(name, rating, side, goals)
Forward(name, rating, assists, goals)
Team(name, club, price)

Which ONE of the following relational algebra expressions checks that every name occurring in Team appears in either Defender or Forward, where $\phi$ denotes the empty set?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 11)

Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h3pJZbed9M8&t=596s

Concept:

$R - S = \phi$ if and only if $R \subseteq S.$

Or

$R \subseteq S $ if and only if $ R - S = \phi$

Understanding from Cricket point of view:

Assume: Defender = Batsmen ; Forward = Bowler ; Team = Final-11 Indian Team

Option A: Every player in the Team is an Alrounder.

Option B: Every Alrounder is in the Team.

Option C: Every player in the Team is either a Batsman or a Bowler (or Both).

Option D: Every Batsman, Every Bowler is in the Team.

So, our answer is Option C.

questions.qtext:
In a relational database there are three relations:

  • $Customers = C\textsf{(CName)}$,
  • $Shops = S \textsf{(SName)}$,
  • $Buys = B\textsf{(CName, SName)}$.

Which of the following relational algebra expressions returns the names of shops that have no customers at all? [Here $\Pi$ is the projection operator.]
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 3)

Let's go option-wise,

Option A).Πsname B will direct project shop names with at least one customer.

Option B). Here we are performing a set difference between two which are not even Union Compatible.

Option C). Set the difference between All shop names and shop names with at least one customer, so we will get those with no customers at all.

Option D). This will give those shop names in which all customers bought something. Basically, this is how division operations are written in the Relational Algebra.

Hence, Option C is correct.
